suspected.title: Private dollar issuers holding government debt
suspected.summary: Two private companies, Tether and Circle, issue most of the dollar tokens used in crypto markets, and they back those tokens mainly by buying short-term US government debt. The Bank for International Settlements counted dollar stablecoin assets above 270 billion dollars by December 2025, and about 35 billion dollars of US Treasury bills bought during 2025, which its researchers say is comparable to the largest US government money market funds. Tether's own quarterly attestation for the second quarter of 2025 claimed more than 127 billion dollars of US Treasury exposure. A BIS working paper by Rashad Ahmed and Inaki Aldasoro estimates that a 3.5 billion dollar inflow pushes the three-month Treasury bill yield down by roughly 4 to 5 basis points within two weeks, and that the effect runs larger during redemption episodes. The BIS Annual Economic Report 2025 says over 99 percent of stablecoins are dollar-denominated and that they fail its tests of singleness, elasticity and integrity. An IMF departmental paper, Understanding Stablecoins, published 2 December 2025, warns the same instruments can speed currency substitution and let money cross borders around capital controls, which would cut into what a central bank can steer.

The BIS in Basel produced both the working-paper estimate of the yield effect and the 2025 Annual Economic Report chapter judging stablecoins unfit as the mainstay of the monetary system.

suspected.established: Dollar stablecoin assets exceeded 270 billion dollars by December 2025 and the sector bought roughly 35 billion dollars of Treasury bills in 2025 (BIS). The BIS estimate of the price effect on short-dated Treasury bills is published and peer-reviewed within the BIS working paper series. Over 99 percent of stablecoins are dollar-denominated (BIS Annual Economic Report 2025). Tether itself published a figure above 127 billion dollars of Treasury exposure for Q2 2025. The IMF has stated in a departmental paper that dollar stablecoins may accelerate currency substitution and weaken control over capital flows, and that the risk is larger where inflation is high and confidence in the domestic monetary framework is low. The US enacted a federal stablecoin statute in 2025.
suspected.not_established: That any central bank has actually lost monetary control to stablecoins. The IMF paper argues in terms of regions and country characteristics, not named countries, and publishes no country-level estimate of stablecoin-driven dollarisation; the yield result is an estimate from one BIS working paper by two authors, Ahmed and Aldasoro, using token-blockchain level flow data, and is not an official BIS position. Tether's reserve figures come from attestations commissioned by Tether, not from an audit, so the composition and custody of the Treasury holdings rest on the issuer's own disclosure. Nobody has shown where those bills sit in the US primary-dealer chain, which would determine what a large redemption wave does to the Treasury bill market. The adoption side is the weakest link: there is no public, country-by-country measurement of stablecoin balances held by residents, so the substitution claim cannot be tested.
suspected.test: Two obtainable artefacts. First, a full financial-statement audit of Tether and Circle reserves, with CUSIP-level Treasury holdings and named custodians, which the GENIUS Act's reporting and examination regime should begin to force out of US-licensed issuers. Second, a central bank publishing resident stablecoin holdings as a line in its monetary statistics or balance-of-payments reporting, alongside deposits, for one high-inflation economy; that single series would turn currency substitution from an inference into a measurement.

suspected.body:
Two private companies, Tether and Circle, issue most of the dollar tokens used in crypto markets and back them with short-term US government debt. Their customers buying in or cashing out therefore pushes on the rate the US government pays to borrow, and so on what banks charge everyone else. The tokens also let people in high-inflation countries hold dollars beyond their own central bank's controls on money leaving the country, and nobody counts how many do.

The Bank for International Settlements counted dollar stablecoin assets above 270 billion dollars by December 2025 and about 35 billion dollars of US Treasury bills bought during 2025. Tether's own attestation for the second quarter of 2025 claimed more than 127 billion dollars of US Treasury exposure. A BIS working paper by Rashad Ahmed and Inaki Aldasoro estimates that a 3.5 billion dollar inflow pushes the three-month Treasury bill yield down by roughly 4 to 5 basis points, a basis point being one hundredth of a percentage point, within two weeks. An IMF departmental paper, Understanding Stablecoins, published 2 December 2025, says the instruments can speed currency substitution and move money around capital controls.

No central bank has been shown to have lost monetary control to stablecoins. The IMF paper argues in terms of regions and country characteristics, not named countries, and gives no country-level estimate of stablecoin-driven dollarisation. The yield result is an estimate from one working paper by two authors, Ahmed and Aldasoro, and is not an official BIS position. Tether's reserve figures come from attestations it commissioned, not an audit, so composition and custody rest on the issuer's own disclosure. Nobody has shown where the bills sit among the banks that trade Treasury debt directly with the government, which decides what a large wave of cashing out does to that market. There is no public, country-by-country measurement of resident stablecoin balances, so the substitution claim cannot be tested.

Two records would answer it: a full audit of Tether and Circle reserves naming each bond and custodian, which the GENIUS Act's examination regime should force out of US-licensed issuers, and one high-inflation country publishing resident stablecoin holdings in its monetary statistics.

suspected.title: Buyout funds taking over the companies that make cash
suspected.summary: The firms that print banknotes and supply the inks and threads that make them hard to copy are being bought by private owners who do not have to publish much. De La Rue, which says it supplies finished banknotes, polymer and security features for more than 69 national currencies and passports for 40 countries, and which bought the Bank of England's own Debden printing works in 2003, was taken over by the US private investment firm Atlas Holdings for 263 million pounds; the deal completed on 3 July 2025 and the company left the London Stock Exchange. Before that, in October 2024, De La Rue agreed to sell its authentication business to the US-listed Crane NXT for 300 million pounds. The ink side of the chain is also privately held: SICPA, a family-owned Swiss company that makes security inks for currencies and documents, was found corporately liable by the Swiss Office of the Attorney General in April 2023 for failing to prevent its staff bribing foreign officials in the Colombian and Venezuelan markets between 2009 and 2011, and paid 81 million Swiss francs; it had paid 135 million francs to Brazilian authorities in 2021. The result is that several governments' note supply now sits inside companies that file no listed-company accounts.

suspected.established: The ownership changes and the prices are documented: Atlas Holdings' 263 million pound acquisition of De La Rue completed 3 July 2025 with delisting, and the 300 million pound sale of the authentication arm to Crane NXT was agreed in October 2024. De La Rue's own description of its reach (69-plus currencies, passports for 40 countries, purchase of the Bank of England's Debden operation in 2003) is on the public record. SICPA's corporate liability finding, the 81 million Swiss franc total and the 135 million franc Brazilian settlement were announced by the Swiss Office of the Attorney General and reported by SWI swissinfo.ch, and SICPA published the prosecutor's side letter on its own site.
suspected.not_established: That private ownership changes what central banks pay, what they get, or how securely note supply continues. No regulator or audit office has published a review of the consequences of the De La Rue sale for the central banks that depend on it; the UK government has published no national-security assessment of it that these sources show. The number of central banks with a single-supplier dependency is not published anywhere, because note contracts are almost always confidential. Market-share figures for security ink do not exist in public form: the SICPA reporting does not give one. And there is no evidence linking the ownership change to any conduct problem; the SICPA case concerns 2009 to 2011 employee conduct, not its owners' structure.
suspected.test: The procurement record. A freedom-of-information release of a central bank's banknote supply contract and tender evaluation (the Bank of England's Debden arrangement is the cleanest target, since the works were sold by the Bank itself), showing price, term, single-source justification and change-of-control clauses, before and after July 2025. Alongside it, the UK government's Investment Security Unit record of whether the Atlas acquisition was called in for review. Those two documents would show whether anyone in government examined the dependency, and what the ownership change cost.

suspected.title: Central banks run as state investment funds
suspected.summary: Some central banks have stopped being only guardians of reserves and started acting like state investment funds, deciding where public money is put to work. In March and April 2020 the Saudi central bank, SAMA, moved 150 billion riyals, about 40 billion dollars, of foreign-currency reserves to the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund; Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan said the transfer helped cause the fastest fall in net foreign assets in two decades and that it followed a comprehensive study. In Hong Kong the Monetary Authority's Exchange Fund held 4,161.2 billion Hong Kong dollars at the end of 2025, of which a Long-Term Growth Portfolio of 578.4 billion included 417.1 billion in private equity and 161.3 billion in real assets, with the benchmark set by the Financial Secretary in consultation with an advisory committee and tactical decisions delegated to the Authority. In Nigeria the central bank took the opposite route and ran lending programmes itself: Governor Olayemi Cardoso told the Chartered Institute of Bankers in November 2023 that the bank had pumped over 10 trillion naira into the economy through quasi-fiscal interventions, that this 'took it into areas where it had limited expertise', and that it would stop. In each case the body that sets the price of money is also choosing assets, companies or sectors.

suspected.established: The Saudi transfer amount, timing and the finance minister's confirmation are documented (reported by Bloomberg's Vivian Nereim, carried by Al Jazeera, with Al-Jadaan's statement in the Saudi Press Agency). The HKMA's portfolio figures and the division of decision rights between the Financial Secretary, the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and the Authority are published in the HKMA's own 2025 annual report chapter on reserves management. Cardoso's statements on the scale and withdrawal of CBN quasi-fiscal activity are on the record from his November 2023 keynote, including a 629 billion naira Anchor Borrowers disbursement in 2022 and a 1 trillion naira manufacturers' facility from April 2020.
suspected.not_established: Whether any of this has changed monetary policy decisions. Nobody has shown a case where a central bank softened or tightened policy to protect the value of assets it or a related state fund holds; that is the claim the pattern would need and it is unproven. The Saudi case has no published governance trail: there is no account of who authorised the transfer inside SAMA, on what terms, or whether it is reversible, and the reporting rests on one Bloomberg story plus a short ministerial statement. For Hong Kong, the Exchange Fund's private-equity holdings are disclosed in aggregate only, with no fund managers, vintages or counterparties named, so overlap with institutions the HKMA regulates cannot be checked. For Nigeria, the loan-level record of the intervention schemes, including who received the money and what was repaid, has not been published.
suspected.test: A reserve-transfer paper trail and a holdings list. For Saudi Arabia: SAMA board minutes or the government decision authorising the 150 billion riyal transfer, plus the accounting treatment in SAMA's audited statements. For Hong Kong: the Exchange Fund's Long-Term Growth Portfolio schedule of fund commitments and co-investments by manager, the kind of list US public pension funds publish routinely. Either document would show whether the investing arm and the regulating arm touch the same counterparties.

suspected.title: Central banks building payment routes around Western banking
suspected.summary: Two central banks under sanctions have been connecting their national payment plumbing to each other, and a third has opened a currency channel on the side. Iran's central bank governor Mohammadreza Farzin announced in late January 2023 that Iran's SEPAM financial messaging service had been linked to SPFS, the Bank of Russia's messaging system, after Iranian banks had been cut off from SWIFT; Iran said all of its several dozen financial institutions could connect to Russian banks, and more than 100 banks in 13 other countries already had SPFS access. The card networks followed: a second phase of the Shetab-Mir integration, allowing Russian cardholders to pay by phone in Iran, was launched at a ceremony hosted by the Central Bank of Iran on 13 May 2025, where Farzin said that 'through the SEPAM system, we can connect with any country's banking messaging platform without relying on SWIFT'. In India, the Reserve Bank of India approved a rupee settlement mechanism in 2022 and nine Russian banks opened special vostro accounts with Indian banks under it. The US Treasury, designating Russia's VTB Bank on 14 September 2026, said VTB had built a settlement system using correspondent accounts in Iranian rials and Russian roubles and had moved billions of frozen Iranian assets.

Hamidreza Azizi of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs said the Russian system will not become a viable SWIFT alternative in the short term without China and India, and doubted that non-Russian SPFS banks would take on Iran-related risk; Esfandyar Batmanghelidj of the Bourse and Bazaar Foundation said rouble and rial liquidity is lacking and called the link a step, not a game-changer. The Central Bank of Iran's own deputy for international affairs, Mohsen Karimi, said connection only means communication until banks actually deal with each other. Neither central bank publishes rial-rouble transaction volumes, and the share of trade settled in national currencies is not available. Treasury's 'billions' figure for moved Iranian assets is an allegation in a designation notice with no published evidence attached and no court finding; VTB's response is not in these sources.

Either central bank publishing monthly SEPAM-SPFS message counts and rial-rouble settlement values, or the Bank of Russia's SPFS traffic statistics broken down by counterparty country, would show whether this is plumbing in use or a signed protocol. Failing that, an unsealed US enforcement action with transaction records, or India's RBI publishing drawdowns on the special vostro accounts, which it collects from the authorised banks.

suspected.title: Public digital money that can watch and restrict spending
suspected.summary: When a central bank issues digital money, someone has to decide what the system can see and what it can block, and those decisions are being made now, inside draft laws and technical designs. The European Data Protection Board and the European Data Protection Supervisor, in Joint Opinion 02/2023 on the digital euro regulation, found that the ECB's settlement infrastructure would centrally store data on everyone using the online digital euro, including authentication data, and asked for a binding duty to pseudonymise transaction data towards the ECB and national central banks. The same opinion said the proposed central fraud detection mechanism in Article 32 lacked foreseeability and that its necessity had not been demonstrated, and it welcomed the proposal's ban on programmable money, warning that 'a programmable digital euro would raise unacceptable high data protection risks'. China has taken the other route openly: Mu Changchun, director of the People's Bank of China's Digital Currency Research Institute, described the e-CNY principle as controllable anonymity, summarised as small amounts anonymous, large amounts traceable, with phone-number-only wallets capped at 2,000 yuan per transaction and big-data analysis available to flag suspect wallets for referral to law enforcement. The design choice, not the currency, is what determines whether a payment can be traced or limited.

suspected.established: The EU documents are public and specific: central storage of online digital euro user data including authentication data (para 53), the request for binding pseudonymisation towards the ECB and national central banks (para 54), the finding that necessity of a general fraud detection mechanism was not sufficiently demonstrated (para 60), and the warning on programmability (para 48). On the Chinese side, Mu Changchun's explanation of controllable anonymity was given at the China Development Forum in March 2021 and the PBoC's July 2021 English white paper uses the term managed anonymity; the 2,000 yuan single-transaction cap on phone-number wallets and the referral-to-law-enforcement route are described in the same material, compiled by Stanford's DigiChina.
suspected.not_established: That surveillance or spending restriction has actually been used. No regulator, court or inquiry has published a case of a central bank tracing an individual's digital-currency payments or blocking a category of spending. The EU material is advisory commentary on a legislative proposal that has not been adopted in final form, so the ECB's eventual data architecture is unknown. On the Chinese side the public account comes from officials and from one DigiChina analysis by Eli MacKinnon, who argues small-wallet anonymity is incomplete because phone numbers are tied to government IDs; there is no independent technical audit of what the PBoC can resolve from e-CNY ledger data, and the claim that recipients cannot see payer data has not been verified outside PBoC statements.
suspected.test: A technical specification plus a disclosure log. For the euro area: the ECB's digital euro data protection impact assessment and the final settlement-infrastructure data model, published in full, showing which fields reach the central ledger. For China: an e-CNY law-enforcement request transparency report, or an independent protocol audit of the wallet tiers, showing what can be linked to a person and how often it was. Either would replace official assurance with a checkable record.

Cash leaves no record and buys anything. Digital money issued by a central bank can be built to log who paid whom, and to refuse some payments. Whoever writes the design settles that once for everyone, and the choice is being made now inside draft laws and technical specifications.

In the European Union, the European Data Protection Board and the European Data Protection Supervisor, the EU's data-rules watchdogs, issued Joint Opinion 02/2023 on the digital euro regulation. They found that the European Central Bank's settlement infrastructure would centrally store data on everyone using the online digital euro, including authentication data (paragraph 53), and asked for a binding duty to pseudonymise transaction data towards the ECB and national central banks, meaning strip the names from it (paragraph 54). They welcomed the proposal's ban on programmable money, money restricted to certain uses, warning that a programmable digital euro would raise unacceptable high data protection risks (paragraph 48). Mu Changchun, director of the People's Bank of China's Digital Currency Research Institute, described the e-CNY principle at the China Development Forum in March 2021 as controllable anonymity, summarised as small amounts anonymous, large amounts traceable, with phone-number-only wallets capped at 2,000 yuan per transaction and big-data analysis available to flag suspect wallets for law enforcement.

No regulator, court or inquiry has published a case of a central bank tracing an individual's digital-currency payments or blocking a category of spending. The Chinese account comes from officials and from one analysis by Eli MacKinnon for Stanford's DigiChina, who argues small-wallet anonymity is incomplete because phone numbers are tied to government IDs. suspected.title: Central banks paying the government's bills through overdrafts
suspected.summary: When a government cannot sell its bonds, its central bank can simply credit the treasury's account, and two large African economies have done so on a scale that shows up in the central bank's own accounts. The Bank of Ghana stated in a press release of 9 February 2023 that as at December 2022 it had bought 7.2 billion cedi of treasury bonds from banks, on-lent 8.9 billion cedi of IMF facilities to the government and extended a 37.9 billion cedi overdraft 'solely meant for the purpose of addressing auction shortfalls and paying customers whose bonds had matured', with its net claims on government rising 44.5 billion cedi in the year; it said Ghana had lost access to international capital markets, that the IMF viewed the arrangement as sub-optimal but temporary, and that Parliament had suspended the Fiscal Responsibility Act 2018 and not reinstated it. The Bank then reported a loss for 2022; press reports put it at 60.8 billion cedi, and the Bank itself described a 55.12 billion cedi loss in equity, largely caused by the government's Domestic Debt Exchange Programme, which put a 50 per cent haircut on its own holdings of government paper. Press reports put the Bank's loss for 2022 at 60.8 billion cedi. In Nigeria the Central Bank advanced about 23.7 trillion naira under the Ways and Means facility, although section 38 of the CBN Act caps advances at 5 percent of the previous year's actual revenue and requires repayment by the end of the fiscal year; the government asked the National Assembly to convert the stock into a 40-year loan at 9 percent interest. Governor Olayemi Cardoso has said the law bars further such advances.

The legality of Nigeria's overrun is contested by commentators rather than settled: the breach is asserted by analysts including Kalu Aja and by press reporting of experts calling the bond issue illegal, and no court or audit institution has ruled on it in these sources. suspected.title: Reserve gold that is lent out while still counted as reserves
suspected.summary: Central bank gold is reported as a reserve asset even when the metal has been deposited with or lent to someone else. The IMF's reserves reporting template puts the entry as 'Gold (including gold deposits and, if appropriate, gold swapped)' on a single line, with no separate line for gold lent out or for where the metal physically sits. In January 2025, as bullion was shipped to New York ahead of possible US tariffs, Reuters reported that London market participants were queuing to borrow gold from central banks that store bullion at the Bank of England, and that one source put the minimum wait to withdraw metal from the Bank at four weeks against a normal few days; the Bank declined to comment, and Robert Gottlieb, former head of precious metals at Koch Supply and Trading, said the Bank was 'not prepared to handle the onslaught of gold borrowing'. The ownership question is not new: Germany's Federal Court of Auditors called for a thorough audit of Bundesbank gold stocks held with the Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and the Bank of France, after which the Bundesbank moved to bring metal home from Paris. A reader of the published reserve figures cannot tell how much of the gold is on loan.

suspected.title: The short list of banks the central bank trades with
suspected.summary: Most big central banks and debt offices buy and sell government bonds only with firms on a published short list. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York publishes its primary dealer list itself; after NatWest Markets Securities Inc. withdrew with effect from 16 October 2026 it held 25 firms, including J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Citigroup Global Markets Inc., Mizuho Securities USA LLC and Santander US Capital Markets LLC. To join, a broker-dealer needs at least $50 million of net regulatory capital (a bank, $1 billion of Tier 1 capital at holding-company level) and at least a 0.25% share of Treasury market-making activity, and must then bid for its pro-rata share of every Treasury auction at reasonably competitive prices; the United Kingdom runs the same arrangement through the Debt Management Office, which lists 19 Gilt-edged Market Makers (15 wholesale, 3 associate, 1 retail) and calls them "primary dealers in UK government bonds". Membership can also carry lending access: the Fed's Primary Dealer Credit Facility, announced 16 March 2008 and closed 1 February 2010, was an overnight loan facility for primary dealers only, a discount window for firms that are not deposit-taking banks. Competition authorities have since fined firms on these lists over what their traders typed to each other: on 21 February 2025 the UK Competition and Markets Authority fined Citi 17.16 million pounds, HSBC 23.4 million, Morgan Stanley 29.7 million and Royal Bank of Canada 34.2 million, 104.46 million pounds in total, for one-to-one Bloomberg chats about gilt pricing between 2009 and 2013 that touched DMO auctions, secondary trading and Bank of England buy-back auctions, with Deutsche Bank given immunity for reporting it. On 20 May 2021 the European Commission fined UBS 172,378,000 euros, Nomura 129,573,000 euros and UniCredit 69,442,000 euros over a euro-area government bond trading cartel of 2007-2011 run mainly in Bloomberg chatrooms, with NatWest (then RBS) immune for revealing it; and on 14 September 1992 Salomon Brothers Inc. paid the US government about $27.8 million, part of a $290 million settlement with the Justice Department and the SEC, to settle charges that it limited the supply of May 1993 two-year notes, without admitting a violation.

suspected.established: The lists are public and the criteria are written down. The New York Fed publishes its primary dealer list and the business standards for joining it, including the $50 million net regulatory capital floor for broker-dealers, the $1 billion Tier 1 floor for banks, the 0.25% market-making share, and the duty to bid for a pro-rata share of every Treasury auction; after NatWest's withdrawal effective 16 October 2026 the list names 25 firms. The DMO publishes 19 GEMMs and describes them as primary dealers in UK government bonds. The Primary Dealer Credit Facility, 16 March 2008 to 1 February 2010, lent overnight to primary dealers only. Three enforcement outcomes are documented with dates and amounts: the CMA's 21 February 2025 settlement decision (104.46 million pounds across Citi, HSBC, Morgan Stanley and RBC; Deutsche Bank immune; payment due 22 April 2025), the European Commission's 20 May 2021 decision (UBS, Nomura and UniCredit fined 371 million euros; NatWest immune; Bank of America, Natixis and Portigon found to have taken part but not fined), and the 14 September 1992 Salomon Brothers settlement of about $27.8 million, part of a $290 million package announced in May 1992.
suspected.not_established: That a closed list causes collusion is not established, and the US courts have gone the other way. Private plaintiffs alleging that primary dealers rigged Treasury auctions lost: the Southern District of New York dismissed the claims and the Second Circuit affirmed on 1 February 2024, calling the chatroom messages "inconsequential market chatter" and the plaintiffs' statistics not specific to the defendants. The CMA itself made no finding that the gilt conduct actually restricted competition, only that it was restrictive by object, and the Debt Management Office, the Bank of England, HM Treasury and Bloomberg were not under investigation. No authority has found that any of these conduct findings resulted from the existence of the dealer list, and no enforcement action names a central bank as a party. The official case for a short list is operational: the New York Fed says primary dealers are simply its trading counterparties, that the relationship is a business one and not an endorsement, and it requires back-office capacity, triparty and central-counterparty arrangements and geographically dispersed disaster recovery; the IMF working paper by George Iden and Marco Arnone (March 2003) reports broad agreement among surveyed authorities that such systems are highly recommended. The euro area is the clearest counter-example to the "club" reading: the Bank of Spain's explanation of Eurosystem counterparties sets out only generic criteria (minimum reserve requirements, harmonised supervision, financial soundness, operational requirements) and says the Eurosystem endeavours to have as many bidding counterparties as possible. I did not obtain a count of Eurosystem counterparties, nor the Bank of England's own Sterling Monetary Framework participant list, so no figure is given for either.

suspected.body:
Governments borrow by selling bonds, and central banks buy and sell them to steer interest rates. Both usually deal only with firms on a published short list. Those firms see the state's orders first, and the auction prices decide what a government pays to borrow, which feeds into taxes and mortgage rates.

The New York Fed publishes its list of primary dealers; after NatWest Markets Securities Inc. withdrew with effect from 16 October 2026 it held 25 firms. Joining requires $50 million of net regulatory capital, or $1 billion of Tier 1 capital for a bank, plus a 0.25% share of Treasury market-making. On 21 February 2025 the UK Competition and Markets Authority settled with Citi for 17.16 million pounds, HSBC 23.4 million, Morgan Stanley 29.7 million and Royal Bank of Canada 34.2 million, 104.46 million pounds in all, over one-to-one Bloomberg chats on gilt pricing between 2009 and 2013. Two earlier cases ended similarly: about $27.8 million from Salomon Brothers on 14 September 1992, 371 million euros from UBS, Nomura and UniCredit on 20 May 2021.

That the short list causes the conduct is not established, and US courts went the other way: the Southern District of New York dismissed claims that primary dealers rigged Treasury auctions and the Second Circuit affirmed on 1 February 2024, calling the chatroom messages "inconsequential market chatter". The CMA found the gilt conduct restrictive by object, not that it actually restricted competition, and the Debt Management Office, Bank of England, HM Treasury and Bloomberg were not investigated. No enforcement action names a central bank. The New York Fed says primary dealers are simply its trading counterparties and the relationship is not an endorsement; an IMF working paper by Iden and Arnone (March 2003) found authorities broadly agreed such systems are recommended; and the Bank of Spain says Eurosystem criteria are generic and the Eurosystem aims for as many bidders as possible. No Eurosystem count and no Bank of England Sterling Monetary Framework list were obtained.

Release of the CMA's and the Commission's non-confidential decisions would name the desks, chats and auctions. Dealer-level FR 2004 position reports, filed weekly with the New York Fed and matched against Treasury auction allotments by bidder class, would show what share of each auction the 25 firms take.

suspected.summary: Some of the rooms central bankers sit in publish a guest list and nothing else. The Bilderberg Meetings' own participant list for its 70th meeting, Madrid, 30 May to 2 June 2024, includes "Hernandez de Cos, Pablo (ESP), Governor, Banco de Espana" alongside Poland's finance minister Andrzej Domanski, Turkey's finance minister Mehmet Simsek and US Deputy Treasury Secretary Adewale Adeyemo; Hernandez de Cos was Governor of the Bank of Spain until June 2024, a member of the ECB Governing Council and chair of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, and the BIS announced on 11 November 2024 that he would become its General Manager from 1 July 2025. suspected.established: Named sitting central bankers appear on published lists. The Bilderberg Meetings' own participant list for Madrid, 30 May to 2 June 2024, names Pablo Hernandez de Cos as Governor of the Banco de Espana; the BIS's 11 November 2024 release confirms he held that post until June 2024, sat on the ECB Governing Council and chaired the Basel Committee from January 2019. Central Banking reported on 10 June 2011 that ECB president Jean-Claude Trichet, Belgian governor Luc Coene and Bank of Canada governor Mark Carney were on that year's list. The terms of the gathering are the organisers' own: invitation only, no application, participants attend as individuals, no quoting each other, no votes, no closing statement, and the only documents published are the location, the topics and the list. On the oversight side, the European Ombudsman's case 1697/2016/ANA produced a recommendation dated 15 January 2018 and a decision of 5 July 2018 finding maladministration over the ECB President's membership of the Group of Thirty, with five specific recommendations including that attendance at non-member G30 events meet the same transparency standards as other ECB meetings with the banking industry and that Executive Board members be accompanied by an ECB staff member at all meetings. The rule that exists is the ECB's own: Article 8 of the 2019 Code of Conduct (2019/C 89/03) asks for particular prudence and appropriate safeguards when participating in closed events, Article 7.5 requires written notification of private activities to the Ethics Committee, and the ECB publishes Declarations of Interests and monthly calendars. The attendance is not hidden by the central bank either: the Banco de Espana publishes its governor's institutional diary, and the June 2024 calendar lists "Asistencia al 70 Club Bilderberg" in Madrid on Saturday 1 and Sunday 2 June, in the same list as the European Central Bank Governing Council meeting of 5 and 6 June in Frankfurt. He attended again in 2025, by then as the incoming General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements.
suspected.not_established: Nothing here shows what was said or decided, and nothing in these sources shows a policy that followed from a meeting. The Bilderberg participant list is a list: it carries no agenda item attributed to anyone, no record of discussion and no outcome, and the organisers state there is none to publish. For the Trilateral Commission I could not obtain the Commission's own current membership list from its own website through search, so this record makes no claim that any sitting central banker is a Trilateral member; the only Trilateral facts given are from Britannica. Beyond 2024 and 2011 I did not retrieve the Bilderberg lists year by year, so no series of central bank attendance over time is asserted. The strongest reading in circulation is itself hedged by the researcher who makes it: Lukas Kantor, interviewed in the Georgetown Journal of International Affairs on 24 February 2025, says every ECB president attended at least one conference before taking office but describes his career evidence as largely circumstantial, says he does not want to demonise the meetings, and notes that the subject was almost monopolised by conspiracy theorists, which kept mainstream researchers away. The ECB disputes the Ombudsman's reading directly, calling the G30 an appropriate forum and the group's transparency "certainly adequate"; the Ombudsman's finding concerns the G30, not Bilderberg, and no oversight body in these sources has made any finding about Bilderberg or Trilateral attendance. I found no central bank with a rule flatly barring attendance at such gatherings, only the ECB's prudence-and-notification requirements.
suspected.test: Three artefacts that already exist and are routinely released. First, the monthly calendars and annual Declarations of Interests that the ECB's Code of Conduct requires its Executive Board and Governing Council members to publish, which should show whether a closed meeting was entered in the diary and under what description. Second, the equivalent diaries and expense or travel records of national central banks for the days of a named meeting, obtainable under national freedom-of-information or transparency rules, which would show who travelled, who paid and who accompanied the official, the point the Ombudsman's fourth recommendation turned on. suspected.title: One bank's former staff in Europe's top money jobs at the same time
suspected.summary: In November 2011 several of the most powerful economic posts in Europe and in global financial rule-making were held at the same moment by people whose official biographies record a career at one firm, Goldman Sachs. The European Central Bank's own biography of Mario Draghi, who became ECB President on 1 November 2011, lists him as 'Vice-Chairman and Managing Director at Goldman Sachs International (2002-05)', after ten years as Director General of the Italian Treasury (1991-2001) and before his years as Governor of the Banca d'Italia (2006-2011). The chairmanship of the Financial Stability Board, the body that writes the post-crisis bank rules for the G20, passed in that same month from Draghi to Mark Carney, then Governor of the Bank of Canada, whose Bank of Canada biography records a thirteen-year career with Goldman Sachs in London, Tokyo, New York and Toronto before he joined the Bank in August 2003. In the same weeks, Antonio Borges resigned as Director of the International Monetary Fund's European Department, the desk running the euro-area bailout talks, a post he had held since November 2010; the Financial Times obituary records that he had been deputy governor of the Bank of Portugal from 1990 to 1993 and became vice-chairman of Goldman Sachs International in 2000. Across the Atlantic William Dudley, who joined Goldman Sachs in 1986 and was the firm's chief US economist for a decade, was President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 27 January 2009 to 2018 and chaired two of the BIS central bank committees. Goldman's then chief executive Lloyd Blankfein answered the 'Government Sachs' label in his 2017 shareholder letter by writing that 'five of my most recent predecessors went into government service, and that has not been by happenstance.'

That these posts overlapped in time is a matter of arithmetic on those dates. Goldman Sachs has publicly defended the pattern rather than denied it: Blankfein's 2017 shareholder letter said the firm 'will continue to encourage our people to contribute to government service if they are fortunate enough to be asked'.
suspected.not_established: Nothing in these records shows the people acted together, acted for the firm, or decided anything in its favour, and no source found here shows any instruction, payment or contact between the firm and any of them while in office. The lengths of the Goldman connections are very uneven, which weakens any single label: Draghi was a vice-chairman for three years, Carney spent thirteen years there, while Christodoulou's Goldman jobs were two years as a trader two decades before he ran Greece's debt office, and Issing's listed role is an unpaid-or-paid advisory title with no dates published. The strongest published rebuttal is empirical: David Lucca, Amit Seru and Francesco Trebbi, in Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report No. 678 (June 2014), built career histories for 34,064 current and former staff of US banking regulators and found flows into and out of regulation both rose in periods of intense enforcement, results they say 'appear inconsistent with a quid pro quo explanation of the revolving door' and more consistent with 'regulatory schooling', while cautioning that their evidence is 'admittedly naive' and does not rule out distortions at a finer level. In other words, movement between a big bank and public office may simply reflect where people with that training are recruited from, and a list of names without a base rate does not separate concentration from selection. Josef Joffe's Hoover Institution column of 5 December 2016, which asserts that 'the real locus of power is not the White House, but the Goldman Sachs headquarters', is a short opinion piece with no data and should not be read as evidence. Three cases often cited in this argument were not verified in this round and are deliberately left out: Mario Monti's reported advisory role with Goldman Sachs before becoming Italian Prime Minister in November 2011, and the US Treasury secretaryships of Robert Rubin and Henry Paulson.
suspected.test: A single countable dataset settles the concentration question. Compile, from official central bank and ministry biographies and gazette appointment notices, the prior private employer of every governor of the 63 BIS member central banks, every G20 finance minister and every national debt-office head for 1990 to 2026, then compare the Goldman Sachs share against the shares for Citigroup, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank, McKinsey and the IMF itself, and against each firm's share of senior finance employment. If Goldman's share is not out of line with its size, the pattern is selection; if it is, the number is the finding. The method is already proven: Lucca, Seru and Trebbi did exactly this for 34,064 US regulator CVs.

suspected.title: Thirty governors meeting in Basel with no agenda or record released
suspected.summary: Every two months the governors of 30 of the Bank for International Settlements' member central banks meet in Basel as the Global Economy Meeting, a group the BIS says represents about four fifths of world GDP, with the governors of 22 further central banks attending as observers; a smaller 19-member Economic Consultative Committee, made up of all the governors who sit on the BIS Board plus the BIS General Manager, prepares the proposals and recommends who chairs the three Basel central bank committees. Both bodies are led by the same person: the BIS announced on 12 November 2025 that Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank, would take the chair from May 2026, succeeding Jerome Powell, after Agustin Carstens (from 1 July 2013) and Mark Carney (from 1 December 2017). The BIS page for the Markets Committee, one of the committees the meeting instructs, states plainly that 'there are no public releases of the meeting agendas or discussions'. Papers from these meetings do exist in member central banks: in 2019 the Reserve Bank of Australia, answering a freedom-of-information request about the Global Economy Meetings, refused to release the agendas, discussion papers and meeting programmes under sections 33 and 45 of the FOI Act, its Secretary Anthony Dickman saying release could reasonably be expected to cause damage to the Bank's international relations and that the BIS had supplied the material in confidence; on internal review Assistant Governor Lindsay Boulton upheld the refusal under section 33(b), which covers information communicated in confidence by an international organisation, and released only 54 travel documents showing that Governor Philip Lowe and the RBA's chief representative in Europe, Michael Davies, were the only two officers who attended. suspected.title: One company's risk software inside the banks and the central banks that watch them
suspected.summary: BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, also sells the software that other investors use to measure their own risk. Its platform, Aladdin, held 21.6 trillion dollars of assets from only about a third of its 240 clients when the Financial Times counted in early 2020, and BlackRock had stopped publishing the figure after disclosing 20 trillion dollars in February 2017; by November 2020 the FT reported more than 900 clients in 65 countries. Public bodies are among the users: the Bank of Israel started on Aladdin in 2019 and ran 208 billion dollars of foreign-currency assets on it, according to Central Banking in March 2022, and BlackRock's separate Financial Markets Advisory arm says it has served over 280 clients in more than 35 countries across more than 580 engagements since 2008. Regulators have written about the general shape of this, without naming the firm: the Financial Stability Board's December 2023 toolkit says authorities may conclude that a provider serving many institutions, where switching quickly is impractical, creates a 'systemic third-party dependency', and the Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee said in April 2025 that 'reliance on a small number of providers for a given service could lead to systemic risks'. The worry named by investors is narrower and older: the Los Angeles County Employees' Retirement Association, a 58 billion dollar pension fund, cited the potential for 'groupthink' in January 2020 as one reason it declined Aladdin's risk tools. BlackRock's chief operating officer Rob Goldstein answered that Aladdin's risk tools are 'designed to support, rather than replace, portfolio managers', that rivals exist in 'an incredibly competitive environment', and that the total assets figure does not reflect how clients actually use the platform.

suspected.title: Central bankers trading their own money while setting policy
suspected.summary: In September 2021 newspapers read the Federal Reserve's own annual disclosure forms and found that officials had been trading during the year the Fed was rescuing markets. The Wall Street Journal reported on 7 September 2021 that Dallas Fed president Robert Kaplan made multiple 2020 trades including stakes over one million dollars in Apple, Delta Air Lines and Occidental Petroleum; Bloomberg reported the next day that Boston Fed president Eric Rosengren bought and sold real-estate investment trusts in 2020 while warning publicly about property-market contagion. Both announced their departures on 27 September 2021: Rosengren retired on 30 September citing a worsening kidney condition, and Kaplan left on 8 October saying his financial dealings risked becoming a distraction to the Fed's execution of monetary policy. Vice chair Richard Clarida, reported on 1 October 2021 to have moved between one and five million dollars from a Pimco bond fund into stock funds on 27 February 2020, resigned in a letter to President Biden on 10 January 2022, leaving on 14 January instead of 31 January. The Fed's Inspector General closed both investigations on 18 January 2024: it found no violation by Kaplan, Rosengren, Powell or Clarida of the laws, rules or policies it examined and told the Inspector General there was insufficient evidence to refer anything for law-enforcement review, while saying Kaplan's filing created an 'appearance of acting on confidential FOMC information' and Rosengren's REIT trading an 'appearance of a conflict of interest'. The FOMC adopted new rules on 18 February 2022 banning individual stocks, sector funds, individual bonds, crypto, commodities and foreign currencies for officials and their spouses and minor children, with 45 days' non-retractable notice, pre-clearance, a one-year holding period and no trading during periods of heightened market stress. The pattern is not only American: Swiss National Bank chairman Philipp Hildebrand resigned on 9 January 2012 over dollar transactions he and his wife made in 2011, three weeks after an SNB report cleared him of wrongdoing, and the European Central Bank published an enhanced code of conduct on 16 December 2022 under which Banco de Portugal governor Alvaro Santos Pereira's December 2025 purchases of Galp Energia and Jeronimo Martins shares were found incompatible with the rules and unwound.

The companion report on Board trading, also dated 18 January 2024, found no evidence that Powell or Clarida violated laws, rules or policies then in effect - Powell's five 11 December 2019 trades were made by his spouse as trustee of a charitable lead annuity trust and fell in a blackout the advisers called an oversight; Clarida omitted one trade from his 2019 form and three from his 2020 form, amended both on 16 December 2021, and the OIG found the omissions needed no further investigation - while stating that the rules then in effect 'did not sufficiently support public confidence'. In both reports the OIG consulted experts on federal insider-trading law, including 18 U.S.C. 1348 and Rule 10b-5, and found insufficient evidence to refer the matter for law-enforcement review. A later OIG report dated 4 September 2024 and released on 11 September found that Atlanta Fed president Raphael Bostic breached two FOMC rules and two Atlanta Fed policies, with more than 150 transactions executed on his behalf during blackout periods between March 2018 and March 2023 and Treasury holdings above the 50,000 dollar threshold, while finding the trades were not based on confidential information and showed no conflict of interest; it made no recommendations and referred the report to the Board. Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to all twelve Reserve Banks on 15 September 2021 asking them to ban senior officials from owning individual stocks, and asked the SEC on 1 October 2021 to investigate Clarida's trades. The rules the Fed then adopted, announced by Powell on 21 October 2021 and formally adopted by the FOMC on 18 February 2022, take effect from 1 May 2022, with notice and pre-clearance from 1 July 2022. Abroad: Al Jazeera reported that the SNB cleared Hildebrand in a report in late December 2011 and that he resigned on 9 January 2012 amid public criticism of 2011 dollar transactions by him and his wife that profited tens of thousands of dollars, the details having been leaked by an IT employee at Bank Sarasin; he denied breaking central bank rules and said he would give the profits to charity. The ECB published its enhanced code of conduct on 16 December 2022 for Governing Council, Executive Board and Supervisory Board members, with additional restrictions on private financial transactions.
suspected.not_established: Nobody has established that any of these trades changed a policy decision, and in the US cases the official findings run the other way: the Inspector General found no violation by Kaplan, Rosengren, Powell or Clarida of the rules it examined, made no law-enforcement referral in either investigation, and found that Bostic's trades were not based on confidential information and showed no conflict of interest. The findings against Kaplan and Rosengren are findings of appearance under internal codes, not of law-breaking, and the Dallas Morning News headlined the January 2024 result as the watchdog clearing Kaplan. Rosengren gave a medical reason for retiring and the sources read here do not establish that his trading caused it. Critics who think the matter was not closed include Senator Elizabeth Warren, who wrote to the Inspector General on 5 March 2024 about the report, and the contents of that letter were not read here. The Portuguese case rests on a report in Publico relayed by an English-language outlet: neither Banco de Portugal nor the ECB disclosed the value of the trades or the date they were unwound, and no sanction was announced. On the comparative question the evidence simply stops: no systematic cross-country study of central bank officials' personal trading or of the disclosure rules that cover them was found, and the IMF's Central Bank Transparency Code of June 2020 contains no principle on officials' personal financial interests, only principle 1.6.3 on anti-corruption measures and internal codes of conduct, with conflicts of interest appearing in the consultation feedback rather than in the code.

For the euro area, the ECB's enhanced code of conduct requires high-level officials to declare private financial transactions, and the ECB publishes members' declarations of interests; for the US, Reserve Bank presidents and Board members file annual OGE Form 278e reports, which the Fed releases on request. Collecting both sets for one calendar year, plus the equivalent declarations from the Bank of England, Bank of Japan, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of Australia, would show for the first time which central banks publish their officials' transactions at all and what the officials hold - and the absence of a filing for a given central bank is itself the finding.

suspected.body:
Senior Fed officials know policy decisions before anyone else, and those decisions move share and bond prices; they also hold personal investments, listed on annual forms. In September 2021 reporters found trades made during 2020, while the Fed was buying assets heavily. The Inspector General investigated and on 18 January 2024 found no violation by Robert Kaplan, Eric Rosengren, Jerome Powell or Richard Clarida, and made no law-enforcement referral.

On 7 September 2021 the Wall Street Journal reported 2020 trades by Dallas Fed president Kaplan including stakes over one million dollars in Apple, Delta Air Lines and Occidental Petroleum; Bloomberg next day that Boston Fed president Rosengren traded property funds while warning about property-market contagion. Both left in autumn 2021; Clarida resigned on 10 January 2022. Neither man broke the blackout or conflict-of-interest rules, Kaplan's sales coming from options written before the blackout, though each filing created an "appearance of a conflict of interest". A report of 4 September 2024 found Atlanta Fed president Raphael Bostic breached two FOMC rules and two Atlanta Fed policies, with more than 150 transactions in blackout periods from March 2018 to March 2023, though it found the trades were not based on confidential information.

Nobody has established that any trade changed a policy decision. The Kaplan and Rosengren findings are of appearance under internal codes, not law-breaking; the Dallas Morning News headlined the result as the watchdog clearing Kaplan. Rosengren cited a kidney condition for retiring. Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to the Inspector General on 5 March 2024; that letter was not read here. Two cases abroad are thinner: Swiss National Bank chairman Philipp Hildebrand resigned on 9 January 2012 over 2011 dollar transactions, three weeks after an SNB report cleared him; Banco de Portugal governor Alvaro Santos Pereira's December 2025 share purchases were unwound under the ECB's code, on a Publico report with no sanction disclosed. No cross-country study of officials' personal trading was found, and the IMF's June 2020 Central Bank Transparency Code has no principle on personal interests.

One table from existing filings would settle it: ECB declarations of private financial transactions, the OGE Form 278e reports US Fed officials file, and equivalents from the Bank of England, Bank of Japan and Reserve Bank of Australia. A central bank with nothing to collect is the finding.
